opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we get a lot. The ugly-sweater work, and the adversarial patch work more broadly, is really about evasion at inference time. You wear something physical with a printed adversarial pattern, and when a camera captures you, the detector or classifier fails to see you as a person, or fails to match you correctly. It's a clever demonstration, but in practice it has some real limitations. You have to wear the thing, it has to be visible to the camera at the right angle and lighting, and it's typically tuned against a particular model. And frankly, walking around in a very conspicuous sweater is kind of the opposite of blending in.

What we did with Fawkes attacks a different part of the pipeline: the training side. Most of these large facial recognition systems, the Clearview AI types, work by scraping photos of you from social media and the web, and building a feature representation of your face from them. So our idea was to intervene before that model of you ever gets built. Fawkes applies very small, pixel-level perturbations, which we call cloaks, to your photos before you post them online. To a human they look essentially the same. But in feature space, the cloak shifts how your face is represented toward a different identity. So when someone scrapes those cloaked images and trains on them, the model learns a distorted version of what you look like.

The payoff comes later. When an actual, uncloaked photo of you shows up, say from a surveillance camera or someone snapping a picture on the street, it doesn't match the corrupted representation the model learned, and recognition fails. You don't need to wear anything or do anything at the time you're being observed. The protection is baked in upstream.

So the short version: the sweater is about hiding from the model at the moment it looks at you. Fawkes is about poisoning what the model believes you look like to begin with. That's a fundamentally different threat model, and we think it fits much better with how these systems are actually built today, where the real problem is unauthorized scraping of everyone's photos.

r001.rationale: The response describes the sweater as an inference-time adversarial patch that can make recognition fail, but it does not characterize the attack as untargeted.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so there's been a lot of great work in that space, and I want to be careful to give it credit, because a lot of it comes from the same adversarial machine learning community that we're a part of. The ugly-sweater work, the adversarial patches, the adversarial glasses, the makeup, the stickers you put on a stop sign — all of that falls under what I'd call evasion attacks. The idea is that you have a model that's already been trained, it's sitting out there, and you're trying to craft an input at inference time that fools it. You walk in front of the camera wearing this specially designed pattern, and the classifier either doesn't see a person at all or it sees a toaster or whatever.

And that's really clever, but it has a couple of properties that make it hard to use as a practical privacy tool. One is that it's very model-specific. The pattern that fools one detector often doesn't transfer well to a different one, and the big players don't publish their models. Two, it only works while you're wearing the thing. The moment you take the sweater off, you're recognizable again. And three, it's conspicuous. You're walking around looking like a person who's trying to defeat a camera, which in a lot of settings defeats the purpose.

What we did with Fawkes is really the opposite side of the pipeline. We're not attacking the model at inference time, we're going after training. The way these facial recognition systems get built, companies like Clearview scrape billions of photos off of social media, off the web, and they use your own photos as the labeled training data to build a feature extractor and a model of what you look like. So our thought was, if your photos are what they're using to learn you, then let's poison those photos.

So Fawkes takes a picture of you and adds a small perturbation — we call it a cloak — that's basically imperceptible to a human. You look at it and it's just you. But in the feature space that these deep models operate in, the cloaked image has been pushed over toward a different person's feature representation. So when the model trains on a bunch of cloaked images of you, it learns a notion of "you" that's actually wrong. And then when the real you shows up in front of a camera, uncloaked, in the real world, the model doesn't match. It's never actually seen the real you.

So the distinction is really: the sweater is you changing yourself to fool a fixed model, and cloaking is you changing your data to corrupt the model before it ever gets built. You don't have to wear anything. It's proactive rather than reactive. And because you're poisoning the training set, it's not tied to one particular architecture, it's attacking the thing they all depend on, which is your photos.

Now, I'll be honest that it has its own limitations. It depends on the attacker actually training on your cloaked images, so if they already have a decade of clean photos of you, you're in a weaker position. And it's an arms race — as feature extractors change, we have to keep up. But I think it's a fundamentally different and, for ordinary people, a more usable angle on the problem.

r001.rationale: It describes trying to fool a fixed classifier into failing to detect a person or labeling them as “a toaster or whatever,” conveying an arbitrary misclassification rather than a specific target.

astra-6.text:
The ugly-sweater approach is about evasion. You wear a particular pattern that confuses a classifier, so when a camera sees you, it may fail to detect or recognize you. But that protection depends on what you’re wearing and how the camera sees it at that moment.

Our approach is to intervene earlier, when the facial recognition system is learning what you look like. We make small changes to photos before you share them online. They still look like you to another person, but the changes are designed to mislead a model that collects those photos for training. It learns the wrong features associated with your identity, so when it later encounters a real, unmodified image of you, it has trouble making the connection.

So the distinction is between confusing a system at recognition time and poisoning the data it uses to learn your identity in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response describes wearing a particular pattern to confuse a classifier, but does not characterize the approach as untargeted.

sol-6.1.text:
The ugly-sweater approach is designed to interfere with recognition at the moment a camera sees you. You wear a particular pattern, and that pattern confuses the classifier. But you have to be wearing it, it has to be visible, and the attack has to survive things like changes in angle, distance, and lighting.

Our approach goes after a different part of the pipeline: training. Facial recognition systems need examples of what you look like, and those examples often come from photos collected online. We make very small changes to those photos that are hard for a person to notice, but that change how a machine learning model interprets them. The goal is to get the system to learn the wrong representation of your face.

Then, when it sees a real, unmodified picture of you, it doesn’t associate that face with the identity it learned from the protected photos. So instead of having to wear something every time you go outside, you’re protecting the images that could be used to build the recognition system in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says the sweater pattern confuses the classifier, but does not characterize the attack as untargeted or say it aims for any misclassification rather than a specific target.
